title: Prototype Pattern
oneLiner: Creates new objects by cloning a fully-configured existing one, instead of rebuilding from scratch every time.

hero.name: The Clone
hero.power: Duplicates a fully-configured object instantly, sidestepping expensive or complex construction.
hero.weakness: Cloning gets dangerous with deep object graphs — copy the reference instead of the value, and two 'independent' clones start mutating the same shared state.
hero.origin: The Clone appeared after a game engine spent 40ms rebuilding an identical enemy-goblin object from scratch, a thousand times a second, instead of just copying one already-built goblin.

story.problem: Spawning a new enemy means re-running its entire expensive setup — loading its stats, mesh, and AI config from disk — every single time, even though 999 identical goblins were already built moments ago.
story.solution: The Clone keeps one fully-built goblin around as a prototype. Spawning a new one is just `goblin.clone()` — no reconstruction, no disk reads.
story.result: Spawning goblins goes from a disk-bound operation to an in-memory copy, and every clone starts from an already-valid, fully-configured state.

before: Every new object re-runs expensive setup from scratch
Construction cost is paid again and again for identical objects
No easy way to spawn 'a copy of this, but tweaked'
after: New objects are copied from an already-built prototype
Construction cost is paid once, cloning is cheap
Cloning plus a small tweak replaces re-running full setup

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A profiler shows enemy spawning eating 40ms per goblin, every single spawn.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Why are we reloading the goblin's mesh and stats from disk every time? We already built one two seconds ago!

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Clone steps forward holding a fully-assembled goblin, ready to duplicate.
panels.speaker: The Clone
panels.dialogue: Stop rebuilding from zero. Keep one finished original — I'll copy it instantly, every time you need another.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: goblin.clone() produces a fresh, independent copy in microseconds.
panels.speaker: The Clone
panels.dialogue: Implement clone() once, deep-copying anything mutable inside. After that, spawning is just calling it.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: A thousand goblins spawn in a single frame, no disk I/O in sight.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Spawn time dropped from 40ms to under a microsecond. We shipped the horde level on schedule.

useWhen: Constructing an object from scratch is expensive (disk I/O, network calls, heavy computation) but you need many similar instances.
You want to create objects whose exact class isn't known until runtime, but you have a compatible instance to copy.
You need 'this, but slightly different' instances — clone, then tweak the copy.
avoidWhen: Construction is already cheap — cloning adds an interface (`clone()`) for no real benefit.
The object holds resources that can't be safely duplicated (open file handles, network sockets, database connections).
You can't guarantee a correct deep copy, and shallow-copy bugs would cause subtle shared-state corruption.
commonMistakes: Doing a shallow copy of a nested object graph — two 'independent' clones end up sharing (and corrupting) the same inner array or object.
Cloning objects that hold live resources (sockets, file handles) without re-establishing those resources properly.
Using Prototype where the object is cheap to construct anyway — the cloning machinery isn't worth it.
Forgetting to override default clone behavior in subclasses, so a subclass clone silently loses its extra fields.
explanation.realWorldExample: JavaScript's own prototype-based inheritance, `Object.create()`, cell/document duplication in design tools (Figma's 'duplicate' or a spreadsheet's 'copy row'), and game engines spawning many similar entities all lean on Prototype.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this just... copying an object? Why does it need a pattern name?

conversation.speaker: The Clone
conversation.message: Because naive copying is dangerous. A shallow copy shares nested objects between 'independent' clones — mutate one, and the other silently changes too. I formalize doing it correctly.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So deep copy is always the answer?

conversation.speaker: The Clone
conversation.message: Not always — sometimes sharing an immutable piece (like a mesh that never changes) is fine and saves memory. The skill is knowing exactly what needs its own copy.

codeBattle.scenario: Your document editor needs a 'Duplicate Slide' button. Each slide holds a complex tree of shapes, text boxes, and styles that took real work to construct.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Clone copies the fully-built slide (with a correct deep copy of its shape tree) instantly, instead of reconstructing an equivalent slide from scratch.

quiz.question: What is the core idea behind the Prototype pattern?
options: Create new objects by copying an existing, fully-configured instance
Ensure a class has exactly one instance
Assemble an object through a sequence of named construction steps
Define a family of related object-creation methods
quiz.answer: Create new objects by copying an existing, fully-configured instance
quiz.explanation: Prototype's defining move is cloning a ready-made object instead of building a new one from raw inputs.

quiz.question: What's the most common bug when implementing Prototype?
options: A shallow copy leaves clones sharing the same nested mutable object
The clone accidentally becomes a Singleton
Cloning is always slower than constructing from scratch
TypeScript doesn't allow a clone() method
quiz.answer: A shallow copy leaves clones sharing the same nested mutable object
quiz.explanation: If clone() doesn't deep-copy mutable internals, 'independent' clones end up silently entangled.

quiz.question: When should you avoid Prototype?
options: When the object holds live resources like open sockets or file handles that can't be safely duplicated
When you need to create many similar, expensive-to-construct objects
When you want a copy of an object with a small tweak applied
When the object's exact class isn't known until runtime
quiz.answer: When the object holds live resources like open sockets or file handles that can't be safely duplicated
quiz.explanation: Cloning a live connection doesn't give you a second working connection — those resources need proper re-acquisition instead.

quiz.question: What real-world benefit does Prototype provide over always constructing from scratch?
options: It skips repeating expensive setup work by copying an already-built object
It removes the need for constructors entirely
It automatically validates the cloned object's fields
quiz.answer: It skips repeating expensive setup work by copying an already-built object
quiz.explanation: The whole payoff is paying the expensive construction cost once, then cloning cheaply afterward.
